"The haves and have-nots" is a phrase used to describe the two broad groups that exist in any society, community, or even a workplace:

  • The haves — people who have wealth, power, resources, opportunities, or advantages.
  • The have-nots — people who do not have those same things.

Together, the phrase captures the gap — often a deeply unfair one — between those who are well-off and those who are not.

Think of it like this: imagine two people sitting at a dinner table. One person has a full plate of food, clean water, and dessert waiting. The other person has an empty plate and no certainty of when they'll eat next. The first person is a "have." The second is a "have-not."
Breaking It Down Word by Word

The phrase is built from one of the most ordinary words in English — the verb "to have."

  • If you have something — money, a home, education, influence — you are among the haves.
  • If you do not have those things — if life's basic and better resources are out of your reach — you are among the have-nots.

So the word is literally constructed from "have" and "have not." Simple verb, profound meaning.

This is important. While wealth is the most common thing people think of, "haves and have-nots" can refer to any kind of significant advantage or resource, including:

  • Education — Those who received a good education vs. those who had no access to one.
  • Healthcare — Those who can afford proper medical treatment vs. those who cannot.
  • Technology — Those who have smartphones, computers, and internet vs. those who don't (this is sometimes called the "digital divide").
  • Political power — Those whose voices are heard by governments vs. those who are ignored.
  • Social opportunity — Those born into well-connected families vs. those who must struggle from zero.

In every case, the idea is the same: a clear divide between the advantaged and the disadvantaged.
The Social Weight of the Phrase

The phrase is never neutral. When someone says "the haves and have-nots," they are almost always pointing to a problem — specifically, inequality. It carries a sense of injustice, because the division it describes is rarely about personal merit alone. Often, the "haves" were born into their advantages, and the "have-nots" were born into their struggles.

This is why the phrase is common in:

  • Political speeches — when leaders talk about inequality and economic justice.
  • News articles — when journalists report on poverty, class, or wealth gaps.
  • Social commentary — when writers or thinkers criticize how unfairly a society distributes its resources.
  • Everyday conversation — when ordinary people talk about fairness, opportunity, or life circumstances.
It Describes a Spectrum, Not Just Two Boxes

In reality, there isn't a clean line where "haves" end and "have-nots" begin. Society is a wide spectrum — from the extremely wealthy to the desperately poor, with millions of people somewhere in the middle. The phrase "haves and have-nots" simplifies this spectrum into two groups for the sake of making a clear point about inequality. It's a way of saying: "Look at how wide this gap is."

Here are some real-world-style examples to show how the word is naturally used:

  • "The pandemic made it painfully clear who the haves and have-nots are — those who could work from home, and those who couldn't."
  • "In that city, the haves live in gated communities while the have-nots sleep in shelters a few miles away."
  • "When it comes to quality education, this country is deeply divided between the haves and the have-nots."
  • "The new tax policy does nothing to bridge the gap between the haves and the have-nots."

"The haves and have-nots" is a powerful, loaded phrase that describes the fundamental split in any society between those who enjoy wealth, privilege, and opportunity — and those who are denied these things. It is a shorthand for inequality, and it is used whenever someone wants to highlight how unfairly life's advantages are distributed. The phrase is simple in construction but enormous in meaning — it contains within it the entire story of social class, economic justice, and human disparity.
